lines.note: The example continues Maqifirugayexi from f306: a sudden strong wind and violent waves. Restore the visible paragraph sign, which is also anticipated in the preceding page's catchword.
Ten uo maqi firugayeſu completes the image of waves overturning or enveloping the sky. Taif. is an upright citation label; Lib. 20. belongs to the italic apparatus.

runs.text: Crecendo o vento rijo derepente, as ondas con-

lines.note: The Portuguese translation describes the sudden rise of a strong wind and begins the phrase ondas contrarias. The printed derepente is retained without editorial respacing.
Trarias completes contrarias, describing the waves as enveloping the sky. The historical spelling enuoluião is retained; this ends the quotation begun on f306.
Maqifuſube is smoked leather with a speckled pattern. The following rows explain that the white markings are deliberately left untreated, not accidental defects.

runs.text: algũs ſinais brancos que lhe ficão de propoſito

lines.note: Some white marks remain on purpose. The scan reads algũs, correcting OCR agãs, and the visible abbreviation is not expanded to modern alguns.
Por defumar means left unsmoked, completing the account of the white pattern on the leather. The preposition is por, not OCR par.

runs.text: Certa laya de peça fina enrolada.

lines.note: Maqiguinu is a particular kind of fine cloth supplied rolled up. The scan's broad description does not warrant adding a more specific textile identification.
Maqiire means casting or putting something inside. The scan shows both consecutive i types in maqiire, correcting OCR Maqire and preserving the compound's boundary vowels.
The example puts money into an alms box. The scan reads algũa rather than OCR alaũa; Iifibaconi is the historical spelling of the Japanese box expression, not an anomalous modern initial.

runs.text: Botar dinheiro metendoo na caixa da

lines.note: Iruru completes maqi iruru across the physical line boundary. The Portuguese translates the action as putting money into the box, with the box's purpose specified below.
Eſmola completes caixa da eſmola, the alms box. This short continuation closes Maqiire and should not be attached to the sowing entry below.
Maqimajiye means mixing another seed into what is being sown. The scan reads Semeando, correcting OCR Sencando; the Portuguese object follows below.
Outra ſemente supplies the other seed mixed into the sowing. This continuation is part of Maqimajiye, not an independent agricultural term.
Maqiǒ is equated with Tenguno qiǒ, a demon's book or scripture. Both Japanese long-o marks are carons; the Portuguese gloss uses the dictionary's Christian terminology.

runs.text: Figura em que aparece o demonio pa-

lines.note: A second Maqiǒ denotes an apparition in which a demon appears to deceive someone. Keep the two homonymous entries separate and preserve the divided para.
After completing para enganar, the example begins Maqiǒni xizzu-, sinking into or succumbing to the deceptive apparition. The scan supports a continuous Maqiǒni rather than the OCR's internal space.

runs.text: Ser enganado do demonio com algũa fi-

lines.note: Mu completes xizzumu. The Portuguese explains the result as being deceived by the demon through an apparent form, with figura divided after fi-.
Gura aparente completes the visible or assumed form by which the deception occurs. The row closes the second Maqiǒ entry.
Maqiſoye means enclosing something along with something else. The Portuguese definition starts with wrapping and putting an additional object inside.
The example begins Fumino vocuni, inside a letter. The visible capital F and following u support Fumino, correcting OCR ſumino; the continuation identifies the enclosure.

The example encloses hair or a similar keepsake in a letter. Catamini is the chosen reading of the abraded initial sequence: the t and parts of m are faint, but the surviving strokes and the following cami agree with the Portuguese memorial-gift explanation. This remains a nonblocking reading caveat.

runs.text: barulhar dentro na carta os cabelos, ou outra

lines.note: Completes the printed Em-/barulhar: enclose hair in the letter, or another object. The first vowel is worn; retain the supplied a rather than normalizing this occurrence to the preceding Emburulhar. The damaged b in cabelos retains a faint ascender and bowl and agrees with Japanese cami, rather than OCR caxelos. These damaged letters remain nonblocking caveats.
Couſa por lembrança completes the alternative of another object as a remembrance. This supports the keepsake sense of catamini without replacing the actual printed Japanese by a modern form.
Maqitate here means sowing or scattering. The historical principal form tçuru is retained rather than converted to a modern teru form.
Niuani xiraſuuo maqitatçuru illustrates spreading sand in the courtyard. The Portuguese translation begins with Botar and continues below; xiraſu is the printed Japanese material being scattered.
The Portuguese completes spreading sand in the Niua. Niua is a Japanese courtyard term embedded in the Portuguese explanation and is retained in its printed italic type.
This separate Maqitate means bundling or tying things together. The scan reads Enfeixar, make into a bundle, correcting the OCR's Enfeirar.
The objects are many things gathered together. Vt introduces a Japanese example beginning Sono tçucaneuo, those bundles.

runs.text: totte amatauo fitotçuni xite nauauo mot

lines.note: The example takes many bundles, makes them into one, and uses a rope. Mot is continued as motte below; no terminal hyphen is visible here.
Completes motte and describes binding very tightly. Fab. is an upright citation label; the italic To begins Tomando without a printed line-end hyphen, while the visible abbreviation &c. is preserved.

runs.text: mando muitos molhos, ou amarrados, & fei-

lines.note: Mando completes Tomando: taking many sheaves or bundles. Feitos is divided after the printed fei-, continuing the account of combining them into one bundle.

runs.text: tos em hum feixe amarrandoos muito bem, &

lines.note: The separate bundles are made into one and tied securely. The scan reads amarrandoos, correcting OCR amarrandeos and preserving the printed attached plural object pronoun.
The tying is strong and uses a rope. Camiuo ma- begins a new example involving hair; it is not another reference to paper or bundles.

runs.text: Amarrar os cabelos de detras direi-

lines.note: Completes maqitatçuru: tying the hair at the back straight. Direitos is physically divided at direi-, with the explanation of the hair arrangement continuing below.

runs.text: tos ſem lhe dar dobra como cuſtumão os Iapoẽs.

lines.note: The hair is tied without folding it over, described as a Japanese custom. Preserve the printed Iapoẽs and the Portuguese singular lhe rather than regularizing either form.
Maqitçuqi means winding or clinging around something. The Portuguese era is the historical form for ivy, and the following row supplies its support and another example.

runs.text: na aruore, a cobra, &c. em algũa couſa.

lines.note: Ivy winds around a tree, and a snake similarly coils around an object. The row completes the illustrative definition rather than introducing a separate animal entry.
The Japanese example says snakes welcome contact with something they can coil around. Yoroco- is visibly divided and continues as yorocobite below; Febidomo is retained as printed.
Completes yorocobite maqitçuqu nari, coiling around the encountered object. The Portuguese describes the snake as pleased to find something to cling to, with achar divided after a-.

runs.text: char em que ſe pegar enroſcandoſe, ſe pegou.

lines.note: Char completes achar; the snake clings by coiling itself around the object. The repeated reflexive phrases are retained rather than simplified into smoother modern Portuguese.

runs.text: Pintura de ouro moido em pò.

lines.note: Maqiye is painting or decoration with gold ground into powder. The printed grave in pò is preserved; the definition supplies the material rather than a full account of the technique.

runs.text: O que pinta, ou faz pinturas com

lines.note: Maqiyexi is the person who paints or produces such decoration. The row's Portuguese object is completed on the following line.
Ouro em pò specifies powdered gold as the painter's medium. This short row closes the artisan entry, distinct from the preceding name of the work.
Mara and nancon are alternatives for the male genital organ, glossed here in Latin. The final B. is visibly upright and marks low or vulgar register; it is not part of the italic anatomical gloss.
Mare and marena denote something rare. The alternative marker l remains literal rather than being expanded or confused with the numeral one.
Mareni is the adverb rarely. Adu. and the Portuguese definition are italic grammatical apparatus, while the Japanese headword is upright.
Mari is a ball, and Mariuo qeru illustrates kicking or playing ball. The Portuguese translation begins Iugar à and continues at the top of column 2, not at the page's bottom catchword.
Completes Iugar à pela cõ opè, playing ball with the foot. Mariga fazzumu then introduces the ball's rebound; the Portuguese explanation continues below.

runs.text: torna aſaltar pera cima depois de dar no chaõ.

lines.note: The ball springs upward again after hitting the ground. Enlargement shows a single tilde over the final o of chaõ, correcting OCR chãõ without relocating the mark to modern chão.

runs.text: Sebe pera naõ ſaltar a pela fora.

lines.note: Marigaqi is a hedge or fence that prevents the ball from escaping. The printed naõ places the tilde over o and is retained occurrence by occurrence.
Marobi means falling to the ground. The scan gives Marobi rather than OCR Mirobi; Corobi begins the paired example continued on the following row.

Corobi marobu describes falling flat. Xiga begins the next example about corpses. A small raised ink or type fragment follows Xiga beside the rule, but it does not establish a readable extra letter; it is noted without inventing Japanese text.
Amata marobi yǒte ita says that many bodies lay fallen together. The Portuguese likewise begins many bodies, with corpos divided after cor and no visible terminal hyphen.

runs.text: pos mortos caidos em hum lugar.

lines.note: Pos completes corpos: dead bodies fallen in one place. The scan reads mortos, correcting OCR morios and matching the Japanese corpse example.
Marǒto is equated with Marebito, a guest or outsider. Preserve the caron and the historical Japanese forms rather than replacing them with a modern synonym.

runs.text: Caſtelos, ou cercas que ha na meſma

lines.note: Maru denotes enclosures or subsidiary fortified areas within the same fortress. The Portuguese continues below and should not be read as a claim that each maru is necessarily an independent castle.
Maruga icutçu aruca asks how many such enclosures there are. The Portuguese question begins Quã-, preserving its abbreviation and physical division.

runs.text: tos caſtelos, ou cercas hà na quella fortaleza?

lines.note: Tos completes Quantos: how many castles or enclosures are in that fortress? The printed spacing na quella and the final question mark are retained.
This distinct Maru is glossed Eu el Rey, I the king. The note records the dictionary's first-person gloss without merging it with the surrounding homonyms.

runs.text: Vaſo que ſerue pera ourinar, ou pera

lines.note: A separate Maru denotes a vessel for urination or another bodily use completed below. The historical spelling ourinar is retained without modernization.
Fazer camara completes the chamber-pot definition with defecation. It belongs to the vessel entry rather than describing a room being built.
Marubiôtan denotes round gourds. The circumflex is visible, and the historical biôtan spelling is preserved rather than changed to modern hyoutan.

runs.text: Couſa enuolta como pilouro de ne-

lines.note: Marucaxi is something rolled into a ball, exemplified by a snowball. Neue is divided after ne-, with the Japanese example on the next row.
Ue completes neue. Yuqino marucaxi is a ball of snow; the Japanese example remains upright and is not a term embedded in a Portuguese sentence.
The verbal Marucaxi means making something round. Redonda is divided after re-, and the following example again uses snow.
The round objects are compared to snow formed into balls. Yuqiuo begins the object phrase of the Japanese illustration continued below.
Yuqiuo marucaſu means forming snow into balls. The Portuguese matches that action directly; the historical ſu ending is preserved.
Maruguqe and maruguqeno vobi name a padded, rounded sash or belt. Cingidouro is divided after Cingidou-, with its construction described below.

runs.text: ro a bainhado, redondo, & eſtofado com al-

lines.note: Ro completes cingidouro; the belt is hemmed, round, and stuffed. The chosen reading a bainhado corrects the OCR's rou bainha lo while retaining the visible space after a. The d is weakly impressed and remains a nonblocking caveat.
Gũa completes algũa, specifying something stuffed inside the belt. The abbreviation and physical word division are retained.
Marui means round. The two short Japanese forms that follow are associated adverbial and nominal forms, not missing Portuguese continuation lines.
Marǔ is the adverbial form associated with Marui, round or roundly. It is a genuine short physical row with no Portuguese gloss to supply.
Maruſa is the nominal form, roundness, printed as another short indented row. Keep it separate from both Marǔ and the following verb.
Marumari means becoming round. The Portuguese redonda is divided at redon-, and the example extends the sense to people forming a circle.
Da completes redonda. Ninjuga marumatta says that the people gathered into a round formation; the Portuguese subject A gente continues below.

runs.text: ſe pos em roda, ou em circulo.

lines.note: The people placed themselves in a ring or circle. This translation completes the example rather than adding another verbal principal form.

runs.text: Marume, uru, eta. i, Marǔ naſu.

lines.note: Marume is explained by Marǔ naſu, making something round. The transitive sense contrasts with the preceding intransitive Marumari.
The object is made round; Cuſuriuo maru- begins the example of forming medicine into rounded portions. The printed hyphen divides the verb, not the object word.
Muru completes marumuru, making medicine into pills or little balls. The Portuguese mezinha retains its historical spelling and is not replaced by a modern medical term.
Atoxiqiuo marumete toru introduces taking an inheritance in its entirety. Marumete has a figurative whole or complete sense here, not a literal spherical object.
The Portuguese says to take someone's entire inheritance wholesale. Ata- starts a separate example about the head, continued on the next row.
Mauo completes Atamauo marumuru, shaving the head. The Portuguese continues into becoming shaven or a religious person; its final ra has no visible terminal hyphen.

runs.text: pado, ou religioſo como coſtumão em Iapão.

lines.note: Pado completes rapado, then the gloss mentions becoming a religious person as customary in Japan. The source's explanation is retained without adding a specific order or sect.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de bola que ſeruia

lines.note: Marumono is a kind of ball formerly used as an archery target. The description begins here and specifies the shooting practice in the next row.

runs.text: ãtiguamẽte de barreira a q̃ atirauão com o arco.

lines.note: The ball served as a target at which arrows were shot. The visible abbreviations in ãtiguamẽte and q̃ are retained without expansion.
Marumune describes the smooth, rounded back of a sword blade. Catana is a Japanese sword term embedded in the Portuguese explanation and retains its visible italic type.
Das completes redondas, followed by ſem quinas, without angular ridges. This continuation closes the description of the sword's rounded back.

runs.text: O dormir de noite veſtido, & cin-

lines.note: Marune is sleeping at night still dressed and belted. Cingido is divided at cin-, and the next row supplies a simple Japanese usage example.
Gido completes cingido. Marune ſuru means to sleep in that dressed condition; the Japanese example is separate from the Portuguese gloss and needs no embedded-term marking.
Maruqi is round timber or a log. The Portuguese Pao is retained without adding a modern accent or a specific tree species.
Maruqibune is a boat made from a single log. The wording identifies a one-piece wooden craft without requiring an added technical label in the transcription.

runs.text: Bãbu inteiro, ou q̃ não he quadrado.

lines.note: Marutaqe is whole bamboo, contrasted with squared material. The abbreviated Bãbu and q̃ are source spellings, not transcription omissions.

runs.text: O tecer, ou fazer redondo como

lines.note: Maruuchi denotes weaving or making a round form. The example and the cord comparison follow on the next row.

Maruuchino ſagueuo exemplifies a round-braided cord. The scan restores Maruuchino and ſagueuo from OCR Manuchino ſagucuo; the following page translates the example, anticipated by the catchword Cordão.
